# Interview prep — selling myself & recognising my strengths

For Sanity EM and other roles. Source: CV, [[work/dump/worksummarygpt]], [[work/career/sanity-em-opportunity]].

---

## Recognising my strengths

**I tend to undersell or forget these. They’re true.**

- **Headless CMS & content-as-data is a real speciality.** I didn’t just use Sanity once — I led the migration at Movember (content architecture, modelling, integration). At ROH I’ve shaped content workflows for complex, high-stakes processes (casting) with Prismic and Strapi. I think in structured content and APIs, not just “build a page.”
- **I’m a hands-on leader.** I’m not a manager who stepped away from code. I do architecture, code review, key integrations, and I still care about modular design, composability, and separation of concerns. That’s exactly what “hands-on EM” means.
- **I think in systems.** Flow, supply/consumption, abstraction layers, composability. That shows up in product architecture, content modelling, and how I run teams and workshops (e.g. modularisation of digital architecture).
- **I bridge strategy and execution.** AI product strategy, agency transition, CDN change, workshopped modularisation — I’m not only delivering features; I’m shaping direction and then making it happen.
- **I care about people and culture.** Line manager of 7; hiring, 1:1s, mentoring. I believe happy, motivated developers deliver better products. That’s not fluff — it’s how I prioritise.
- **I’m not dogmatic about tech.** I evaluate ecosystem tradeoffs (e.g. Go vs TypeScript for a side project). I pick tools that fit the problem. That’s useful when leading teams and choosing stack.
- **I have a clear “content + data” throughline.** From Movember (Sanity, content models) to ROH (Prismic/Strapi, casting, content management, AI strategy). Content as real-time, structured data is where I’ve been living.

---

## Selling myself (Sanity EM in particular)

**One-liner:**  
I’m an engineering leader who specialises in headless CMS and content-as-data. I led the Sanity migration at Movember and I shape content workflows and product strategy at ROH. I’m hands-on in architecture and code and I manage and grow developers. I want to help teams treat content as real-time, structured data — Sanity is where that’s happening.

**Why I’m a fit:**
- **Role asks for:** TypeScript, Node, React; hands-on EM; core AI product areas; London.
- **I offer:** All of the above; deep Sanity/headless experience (Movember); content architecture and modelling; dual tech lead + people manager; AI strategy and modular architecture work; contemporary frontend and systems thinking.

**What to say when they ask “Why Sanity?”**  
Sanity has been part of my career since Movember — I drove the migration and owned the content architecture. I’ve been working in headless and structured content ever since. I want to be where content-as-data is the product, not a side project. And I want to lead a team that builds that.

**What to say when they ask “Why move from ROH?”**  
(Adjust to your real reason.) E.g.: I’m not actively looking to leave — I was approached. But Sanity is a rare fit: my speciality (content, headless, structured data), the right level (hands-on EM), and a product I’ve used and advocated for. I’d like to explore it.

---

## Interview talking points (stories to have ready)

- **Sanity / content migration:** Movember — proprietary CMS to Sanity; content architecture, models, integration. Outcomes: brand consistency across touchpoints, reduced dependency on proprietary systems, better workflow and design quality. Be specific: what was hard, what you decided, what you’d do differently.
- **Complex content workflows:** ROH casting — what made it complex; how you shaped the workflow; Prismic/Next.js, Cast Sheet. Emphasise “content as data” and editorial experience.
- **Cross-functional content/CMS:** Worked with architects, content authors, translation, and BAs to align content modelling and workflows with how people work; iterated from feedback. (Shows you don’t just build — you collaborate and adapt.)
- **Hands-on leadership:** A recent example where you designed or reviewed something technical and it shipped. Architecture decision, refactor, or integration you owned.
- **Technical direction / tooling:** You often drove which tools to use and how to conceptualise data and data flow — not just implemented others’ decisions. (Good for “why you’re right for a developer-first product company.”)
- **API / data model ownership:** You designed or owned APIs and data models that other teams depend on: Content, Ballet, Opera, Front of House, Rehearsal, IT (reliability). “Other apps read from here” — you’re the platform others build on.
- **Real-time / multi-channel:** On-sale events for ticket sales — high-stakes, real-time, consistency across touchpoints, performance under load. (Maps to “content as real-time, structured data” and reliability.)
- **Developer experience / how developers work:** Handover between agencies, peer review, branching and collaboration methods, testing tools and workflows, mentoring and coaching reports to improve. (Not just “I mentor” — you’ve shaped process and tooling so the whole team works better.)
- **In-house / agency / offshore mix:** You lead delivery with a blended team (in-house + agency/offshore). Handover, quality bar, and alignment across internal and agency developers. (Common in many orgs; shows you can run mixed models.)
- **Content + AI / product + AI:** Search on RBO; using AI to understand, refactor, and document the codebase; building an AI-driven “external mind” (personal knowledge system). You’ve been in the room defining what AI means for your area — and you’re building it.
- **Cross-functional go-to / content workflows:** Incredibly frequently the go-to for cross-functional work; advocated for internal content workflows; frequent partner to content editors and stakeholders. (Not just “I collaborated once” — you’re the person people come to.)
- **Structured data beyond CMS:** Complex casting data (Opera, Ballet) from enterprise systems; aggregation/cache layer (Pocketbase) for people pages — surgical updates, lower load on large generation tasks. Learning platform and streaming service as multi-consumer data products. (You think in “data for many consumers” even when it’s not called a CMS.)
- **People / growth:** Someone you hired or mentored; how you run 1:1s or feedback; how you balance delivery and growth.
- **AI / strategy:** The AI product strategy at ROH — what you’re driving, how it connects to content/platform. Modularisation workshop — what you workshopped and why.
- **Systems thinking:** How you think about modular design, composability, or separation of concerns. Can use a technical example (e.g. server vs UI state, content APIs) or a process example (e.g. agency transition, branching strategy).

---

## Phrases that work (for me)

- “I led the migration to Sanity at Movember — I owned the content architecture and the integration. It was about brand consistency across touchpoints and reducing dependency on proprietary systems. I educated the organisation on content as structured data and designed the shape of data and the editor experience.”
- “I’m a hands-on tech lead: I’m in the architecture and the code, and I also manage and grow the team.”
- “I think in systems — flow, composability, clear boundaries. That’s how I approach product and architecture.”
- “I’ve often been the one driving technical direction on tooling and how we conceptualise data and data flow — not just implementing someone else’s call.”
- “I’ve designed and owned APIs and data models that Content, Ballet, Opera, Front of House, Rehearsal, and IT depend on — I’m used to being the platform other teams consume.”
- “I’ve owned real-time, high-availability experiences — including on-sale events for ticket sales — where consistency and performance across touchpoints really matter.”
- “I’ve focused on how developers work: handover between agencies, peer review, branching and collaboration, testing workflows, and mentoring and coaching so people actually improve.”
- “I lead delivery with an in-house and agency/offshore mix — so I’m used to handover, quality bar, and alignment across internal and agency developers.”
- “I’ve been in the room for content and product + AI: search on RBO, AI-assisted codebase understanding and docs, and I’m building an AI-augmented knowledge system — so I think about how AI fits into how people actually work.”
- “Content as real-time, structured data is where I’ve been living — Sanity is where I want to help build it.”
- “I worked with architects, content authors, translation, and BAs to fit content modelling and workflows to how we actually work — and iterated from their feedback.”
- “I’m the go-to for cross-functional work — incredibly frequently — and I’ve advocated for internal content workflows; I’m the person content editors and stakeholders come to.”
- “A lot of what I’ve done is structured data and making information usable by many consumers — casting data from enterprise systems, an aggregation layer with Pocketbase for people pages so we could do surgical updates and cut load on big generation tasks, plus learning platform and streaming. It’s not always called a CMS, but it’s the same mindset.”

---

## Before the call (quick checklist)

- [ ] Re-read JD; note 2–3 questions to ask them.
- [ ] Re-read this file; pick 2–3 strengths to mention naturally.
- [ ] Have one “recent hands-on” and one “people/growth” story ready.
- [ ] Know your “Why Sanity?” and “Why this role?” in one sentence each.

# Career advice — growth areas & where to look

Drawn from your CV, [[work/interview-prep]], and our conversations. Use as a running list to reflect on and update.

---

## If you’re not searching right now (e.g. agency transition, modularisation)

**When you *do* have bandwidth to look, focus on:**

1. **One channel** — Don’t spread yourself. Pick one: e.g. one recruiter who gets you (e.g. Jon/Workonomics), or LinkedIn + “Engineering Manager” + “content”/“CMS”/“London,” or 3–5 companies you’d say yes to and reach out direct. Quality over volume.
2. **CV is already there** — You have a Sanity- and content-optimised CV. For other roles, a 5‑minute pass: tweak the summary (content vs generic “platform”), leave the rest. No need to rebuild.
3. **Three stories, ready** — Before you apply anywhere, have down cold: (1) Sanity/content migration + outcomes, (2) one “people” story (hiring, mentoring, or hard conversation), (3) one “stakeholder” story (agency transition, saying no, or cross-functional win). You’ve lived them; just rehearse 2 minutes each.
4. **What you want, one sentence** — So you don’t drift. E.g. “Hands-on EM or Tech Lead where content/data/platform is the product” or “Technical PM in content/CMS.” When a role lands, you can say yes or no quickly.
5. **Let the current work work for you** — Agency transition and modularisation are *great* stories. When you’re in the room later, “I led agency transition and kicked off the modularisation project” is exactly the kind of thing they want to hear. So focus on doing them well; they’ll pay off when you do look.

You don’t need to do anything else until you’re ready. When that is: one channel, light CV tweak, three stories, one sentence on what you want.

---

## Where you are now

You’re an **engineering leader** with a clear **content + data + platform** story: Sanity at Movember (migration, content as structured data, editor experience), ROH (APIs/data models for many consumers, casting, Pocketbase, learning platform, streaming, on-sale, AI strategy). You’re **hands-on** (architecture, code review) and **people-focused** (7 reports, hiring, mentoring, cross-functional go-to). You think in **systems** and **data shape**, not just features. That’s a strong profile for EM, Tech Lead, or Staff roles in content, platform, or product-led companies.

---

## Engineering Manager / Technical Strategist (not “dev”)

You’re **more an engineering manager and technical strategist than a “dev”** — you set direction, own platform/data decisions, and grow teams; you stay hands-on in architecture and review but you’re not targeting pure coding roles. Target jobs accordingly.

### How to target jobs

| What | Look for |
|------|----------|
| **Role titles** | **Engineering Manager**, **Tech Lead** (with reports or “tech lead for product area”), **Head of Engineering** (smaller orgs), **Engineering Lead**, **Technical Lead**. Avoid “Senior Developer” or “Software Engineer” unless the JD is clearly “technical leadership + some coding.” |
| **Job descriptions** | “Technical direction,” “architecture,” “roadmap,” “stakeholder,” “cross-functional,” “grow the team,” “hiring,” “technical strategy.” **Red flag:** mostly “implement features,” “write code 80% of the time,” “no direct reports.” |
| **Your positioning** | Lead with **“engineering leader” / “technical strategist”** who is hands-on in architecture and key technical decisions — not “developer who also manages.” Summary and LinkedIn: “Engineering Manager / Technical Lead” or “Engineering Leader — technical strategy, team leadership, content & platform.” |

### One-liner (for you)

*“I’m an engineering manager and technical strategist: I set technical direction, own platform/data decisions, and grow teams. I stay hands-on in architecture and review, but I’m not targeting pure dev roles — I’m targeting EM, Tech Lead, or technical leadership where strategy and people are the main job.”*

Use this when you’re filtering roles, talking to recruiters, or explaining what you’re looking for.

---

## Areas to think about growing

### 1. **Leadership depth & narrative**

- **Scale of impact:** You’ve managed 7 and led cross-functional work. Next step is being able to say “I’ve grown a team from X to Y,” “I’ve set hiring bar and process,” or “I’ve owned org design for a product area.” If you haven’t yet, look for chances to own one of those (e.g. defining roles, levelling, or team shape).
- **Stories:** Have 2–3 crisp stories: one **technical** (e.g. migration, API ownership, real-time), one **people** (hiring, mentoring, conflict or performance), one **stakeholder** (agency transition, change board, “said no and why”). You’ve got the raw material; practice telling them in 2 minutes.
- **“Why I lead”:** Be able to say in one sentence why you want to lead (not only code). E.g. “I want to multiply impact through others and shape how teams treat content and data.”

### 2. **Scale & “size of problem”**

- You’ve run **on-sale**, **multi-stakeholder** APIs, **migrations**, **agency handover**. If your next move is to a bigger org or a product with more traffic/complexity, start naming scale where you can: “APIs consumed by 6 internal orgs,” “on-sale events with X concurrent users,” “migration affecting Y systems.” It helps interviewers place you.
- **International / multi-locale:** You’ve touched **translation** and **content workflows**. If you want to lean into content/platform, “content for many locales or brands” is a natural next story to collect (even at ROH if it applies).

### 3. **Technical (optional)**

- Your stack (TypeScript, Node, React, Next, AWS, headless) is already a strong fit for content and product companies. **GROQ, GraphQL, or real-time APIs** — if you use them, keep them on the CV; if not, a small side project or internal experiment could give you a talking point for “content APIs” roles.
- **AI/product:** You’re already in the room (search, codebase tooling, external mind). If you want to be “the EM who gets content + AI,” keep doing one concrete thing (e.g. a shipped AI feature or a clear AI strategy doc) so you can point to it.

### 4. **Industry & risk**

- You’ve been in **non-profit/impact** (Movember) and **arts/culture** (ROH). Both are meaningful but can feel “safe” to some employers. If you’re open to **product-led SaaS, content platforms, or scale-ups**, your profile (content-as-data, APIs, real-time, cross-functional) translates well — you may just need to spell out “I’m looking for a place where content/data is the product, not a side channel.”
- **Remote vs London:** You’re London-based. If you’re open to remote-first or hybrid, say so; it widens the pool (e.g. Sanity, other content/CMS companies).

---

If you want to move **closer to product** — more say in *what* gets built, roadmap, discovery, and user/customer outcomes — you have a lot to build on. You’re not starting from zero.

**Purpose:** Low-stakes, fun experimentation; build something small, demo it, learn together. Feeds real experience back into the working group and policy.

**Audience:** Devs first; extend to PMs/others if you run a second round.

**Format (e.g. half or full day):**

- You have a clear brief (work/dump/info-lambda-docs-brief.md). Map its sections to the epic’s “service manual” (getting started, technical, business logic, maintenance, runbook).
